title: Soil temperature

definition.text: How warm or cold a soil is, set by the balance between the energy it absorbs and the energy it loses.

facts.text: Mean annual soil temperature ranges from −10 to 26 °C depending on the biome.
It regulates seed germination, the breaking of seed dormancy, plant and root growth and the availability of nutrients.
It varies by season, month and day, but the swings shrink with depth: upper layers follow air temperature while deeper layers fluctuate less.
Water content, soil colour, relief, cover and air temperature all affect it; paler soils with higher albedo stay cooler than dark ones.
Wet surface soil is typically 3 to 6 °C colder than dry surface soil, because water takes more energy to heat and to evaporate.
Drying or clear plastic mulch raises soil temperature; organic mulch slows warming and damps surface fluctuations.
Farming adapts to it by timing planting, applying anhydrous ammonia below 10 °C (50 °F) and protecting shallow-rooted crops from frost heaving.
Soil temperatures are rising worldwide with climate warming; the main threats concern permafrost thaw, carbon loss and ecosystem collapse.

contested_note: Sources hold opposing views on how warming soils will affect carbon capture, storage and climate feedbacks (S:9d2968b8dea8).
notes: The pilot left the Temperature section of Physical properties of soil to this chapter. White spruce root-growth detail (S:4cea445f4b6b and neighbours) was skipped as too specific.

definition.text: The rate at which heat energy moves through soil in response to a temperature difference between two points.

facts.text: Heat flux density, in W·m−2, is the energy flowing through a unit area per unit time and has both magnitude and direction.
It is calculated from Fourier's law, using the soil's thermal conductivity and the temperature gradient between two depths.
Heat flows against the temperature gradient: when the surface is warmer than the soil below, heat is conducted into the soil.

definition.text: The energy needed to raise the temperature of soil by 1 °C, its specific heat.

facts.text: Pure water has a specific heat of about 1 calorie per gram and dry soil about 0.2, so wet soil lies between 0.2 and 1 (0.8 to 4.2 kJ per kilogram).
Specific heat rises with water content, and evaporating water takes about 584 cal/g (2442 kJ/kg at 25 °C), so wet soil warms more slowly than dry soil.
Volumetric heat capacity, in J·m−3·K−1, is one of the main soil thermal properties.
Liquid water's specific heat, about 4184 J/(kg·K) at 20 °C, is among the highest of common substances; ice just below 0 °C has 2093 and granite about 790.

definition.text: The properties that govern how energy, mostly heat, moves through soil by radiation, conduction and convection, a part of soil physics used in engineering, climatology and agriculture.

facts.text: The main ones are volumetric heat capacity (J·m−3·K−1) and thermal conductivity (W·m−1·K−1); they govern how energy is partitioned in the soil profile.
They change constantly with daily and seasonal cycles, so general statements about one site are hard to make.
Besides basic composition, they depend strongly on volumetric water content and the volume fractions of solids and air.
Soil moisture and thermal properties are so closely linked that they are often measured and reported together.
Surface temperature swings reach deeper layers at reduced rates and with a delay, sometimes called thermal lag.
Uses range from frost effects on construction, buried pipes and cables and the timing of planting to greenhouse gas studies, radioactive waste and locating buried land mines.

title: Soil thermal conductivity

definition.text: The ability of soil to conduct heat, measured in W·m−1·K−1.

facts.text: Typical values in W·m−1·K−1 are 8.8 for quartz, 0.57 for water, 0.25 for organic matter, 0.2–0.4 for dry soil and 1–3 for wet soil.
Air conducts heat poorly and weakens conduction through the solid and liquid phases.
The solid phase conducts best, but varying soil moisture largely determines a soil's conductivity.
Shallow-loop ground source heat pump design needs an accurate in-situ conductivity reading, which a thermal heat probe can provide.

notes: No article; passes the 2+ pages test (Soil thermal properties, Physical properties of soil). Could fold into Soil thermal properties.

title: Thermal lag

definition.text: The damping and delay of temperature changes with depth in the ground, so that deeper soil reaches its highs and lows later and less sharply.

facts.text: About 50% of the Sun's heat is absorbed at the surface, where temperature swings with day and night, weather and season.
Below the surface the ground is warmer than the air in winter and cooler in summer.
Deep enough down, temperature stays constant year round at about the mean of summer and winter temperatures.
Sources vary on that depth: reported values include 5–6 m, 6 m, 15 m, 4.25 m for dry soil and 6.7 m for wet soil.

conflicts.text: Depth of constant ground temperature reported as 5–6 m, 6 m, 15 m, 4.25 m (dry soil) and 6.7 m (wet soil).
conflicts.note: Earth shelter says sources vary for this depth (S:2c3b17b491cb); dry versus wet soil explains only part of the spread.

notes: No article; on Soil thermal properties and Earth shelter.

title: Heat probe method
article: Soil thermal properties#Single and dual heat probes

definition.text: In-situ measurement of soil thermal properties with needle probes that heat the soil and record its temperature response.

facts.text: A single probe heats continuously and senses how fast heat is conducted away, so it measures thermal conductivity only; IEEE 442-1981 and ASTM D 5334-08 cover it.
The dual-probe heat-pulse method uses two parallel needles a set distance apart, a heater and a sensor, and records the sensor's response to a heat pulse over time.
It measures thermal diffusivity and volumetric heat capacity, from which conductivity follows, so it gives all the main thermal properties.
Drawbacks are a small measured volume and sensitivity to probe-to-soil contact and heater-to-sensor spacing.

definition.text: Detecting variations in soil thermal properties from satellites and aircraft, mainly with thermal infrared sensors.

facts.text: Reflected light shows only the topmost few molecular layers; thermal infrared reveals energy variations at shallow depths below the surface.
Thermal sensors pick up heat moving into and out of near-surface layers by conduction, convection and radiation.
Satellite microwave sensing also helps, since unlike thermal infrared it is not affected by cloud cover.

definition.text: Using the ground as a long-term store of heat, carrying solar energy from summer to winter for ground source heat pumps.

facts.text: The thermal effusivity of soil lets the ground serve as underground thermal energy storage.
Design criteria for shallow-loop ground source heat pumps require an accurate in-situ thermal conductivity reading.
In earth-sheltered buildings the thermal mass and thermal lag of the earth keep the need for extra heating and cooling minimal.

title: Soil gas

definition.text: The gases filling the air spaces between soil particles, also called the soil atmosphere.

facts.text: The main soil gases are nitrogen, carbon dioxide and oxygen; nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, methane and ammonia also occur naturally.
Oxygen is critical because plant roots and soil organisms need it to respire.
Gas fills pores as water drains, evaporates or is taken up by roots, so soil air and soil water are often inversely related.
Microbes and roots consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so soil air holds less oxygen and more CO2 than the air above.
Soil organisms emit volatile compounds as metabolites, allelopathic agents and signals, making soil air a network of chemical cues.
Aerated soil is a net sink of methane, but oxygen-depleted soil at elevated temperatures produces it.
Soil is a net emitter of greenhouse gases, especially where permafrost thaws and degasses as the climate warms.
The familiar after-the-rain scent comes when infiltrating rain flushes out the soil atmosphere after a drought.

notes: Facts also draw on Soil#Soil gas, which the what-soil-is pass may use for a section entry.

title: Soil air composition

definition.text: The make-up of the soil atmosphere: similar to the air above, but richer in carbon dioxide and water vapour.

facts.text: A typical comparison gives soil air 79.2% nitrogen, 20.6% oxygen and 0.25% carbon dioxide, against 78.0%, 20.9% and 0.04% in the atmosphere.
In soil pores CO2 may reach 10 to 100 times the atmospheric 0.04%, possibly inhibiting root respiration; at extreme levels CO2 is toxic.
Carbon dioxide increases with depth because of decomposing organic matter and abundant roots.
Calcareous soils buffer CO2 through carbonates, while in acid soils respired CO2 accumulates in the pores.
Composition shifts daily and seasonally with chemical and biological processes, unlike the more uniform atmosphere.
Methane and nitrous oxide are minor but matter for greenhouse gas flux and human impacts on soils.
Temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind and rainfall are important controls on the soil atmosphere.

notes: Soil chemistry (S:666aff6ef8e5) gives 20% oxygen, 79% nitrogen and 0.15–0.65% CO2 under the heading 'In the atmosphere', apparently meaning soil air; not cited. The 0.25% table value and the 10–100 times range are a typical value and a range, so not listed as a conflict.

definition.text: The net movement of gas molecules through soil pores from higher to lower concentration, the main way soil air exchanges with the atmosphere.

facts.text: Gas molecules move constantly and collide in a random walk; diffusion is described numerically by Fick's law.
Oxygen diffuses in from the atmosphere and is consumed, while excess carbon dioxide, other gases and water vapour diffuse out.
Total porosity, pore connectivity, water content, air turbulence and temperature set the diffusion rate, rather than pore size.
The diffusion coefficient falls as soil is compacted, and platy structure also impedes gas flow.
In water-saturated soil, gas diffusion slows some 10,000 times because no open air passages remain.
Short of oxygen, anaerobic bacteria reduce nitrate to N2, N2O and NO gases, depleting soil nitrogen by denitrification.
Daily or seasonal changes in temperature and moisture alter soil gas and so the rate of soil respiration.
Thawing and rewetting of frozen or dry soils boost microbial activity and respiration, causing sudden fluxes of carbon dioxide and methane.

definition.text: The use of soil gases in research on microseepage, earthquakes and gas exchange between soil and atmosphere.

facts.text: Microseepage, the small release of hydrocarbons at the surface, is used to look for petroleum, assuming hydrocarbons migrate vertically.
Migration of soil gases, especially radon, is examined as a possible earthquake precursor.
Landfill waste, mining and petroleum contamination produce gases, including volatile organic compounds, that diffuse through soil.
Fluxes between soil gases and the air can be analysed by distance from the soil surface.

definition.text: The exchange of gases between soil and atmosphere, and the means of improving it.

facts.text: Microbial activity and root respiration deplete oxygen and build up carbon dioxide in the soil, and lack of oxygen can hinder plant growth.
Aeration also allows water drainage and root growth; soil compaction is a common cause of poor aeration.
The pore network ventilates the soil, but it becomes blocked when water fills the pores.
Wind, atmospheric pressure, convection and diffusion all influence aeration rates.
Soil structure strongly affects the larger pores that control aeration, infiltration and drainage.
Waterlogging or compaction that limits aeration can cut nutrient uptake, and bacteria short of free oxygen take it from nitrate.
Liquid aeration applies solutions, commonly of ammonium lauryl sulfate, that break down dense particles and loosen compacted soil.
Liming improves soil structure and thus aeration, and digging megafauna improve it by disturbing soil horizons.

title: Core and spike aeration

definition.text: Mechanical aeration that punctures the soil with spikes or removes cores about 1 in × 2 in (25 mm × 51 mm) to improve gas exchange.

facts.text: Spike aerators use spikes up to a foot or more long and are sometimes used for drainage problems in turf.
Core aeration on turf reduces compaction and thatch, improves infiltration of water and nutrients and encourages deeper roots.
Lawn aerators range from walk-behind, ride-on and tractor-pulled machines to spiked shoes.

notes: S:2c21dd92c22c and S:31d1d26a4f1d carry citation-needed tags.

definition.text: An aeration method that cuts grooves into soil or turf so that water and amendments penetrate and are retained in the right amounts.

facts.text: Organic amendments are spread on the surface, grooves are cut, and the grooves are closed again in the same pass, barely disturbing soil structure.
It can add humus, topsoil, compost, sand or clay as soil softeners where needed.
On lawns it relieves excess water and compaction in heavily used areas, with less surface disruption than coring.

definition.text: The upward swelling of soil in freezing weather as ice grows toward the surface from the freezing front.

facts.text: It needs frost-susceptible soil, a water supply from below such as a water table, and freezing temperatures penetrating the soil.
Water reaches the freezing front by capillary action and feeds growing ice lenses, which can lift soil 1 foot (0.30 m) or more.
Water expands only about 9% on freezing, too little to explain heave; by 1930 Stephen Taber had shown that water migrates to the freeze line.
Taber found that benzene, which contracts on freezing, also heaves, ruling out volume change as the main mechanism.
Differential heave cracks road surfaces, helping form springtime potholes, and damages building foundations.
Cold stores and ice rinks can freeze and heave the ground beneath them; non-susceptible fill, insulation or heating prevent it.
Needle ice is frost heaving at the start of the freezing season, before the freezing front has gone deep.

title: Ice lens

definition.text: A body of ice that grows where moisture diffusing through soil or rock collects in one zone, usually parallel to the surface.

facts.text: Ice first gathers in small pores or cracks and keeps collecting, wedging the soil or rock apart.
Lenses grow several centimetres to several decimetres deep, and their growth is the dominant cause of soil displacement in frost heaving.
They grow by drawing water from groundwater below the freezing line through frost-susceptible soil with capillary pores.
Water in fine pores stays liquid below the bulk freezing point (the Gibbs–Thomson effect), so it can percolate toward the lens.
Rock fracture by ice segregation is a more effective weathering process than the freeze-thaw expansion proposed by older texts.
Arctic tundra favours deep lenses, because permafrost keeps the ground frozen at depth and stops meltwater draining.

notes: The Ice lens article was crawled but sits outside the subject's scope; it carries the mechanism, and the Frost heaving section 'Development of ice lenses' supports the same facts.

definition.text: Soil whose pore sizes and particle surface area promote capillary flow, so that it can feed ice lenses and heave when it freezes.

facts.text: Silty and loamy soils, which contain fine particles, are typical frost-susceptible soils.
Many agencies class material as frost susceptible if 10 percent or more passes a 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve or 3 percent or more a 0.02 mm (No. 635) sieve.
Dense clays, with low hydraulic conductivity, and clean sands and gravels, with pores too open for capillary flow, are not frost susceptible.
Standard tests rate pavement soils by comparing heave rate and thawed bearing ratio with an established classification.

definition.text: Thin films of liquid water that persist on ice below freezing and let fine soil particles migrate through ice toward warmer soil.

facts.text: Faraday reported the unfrozen premelted layer in 1860 and called the particle migration thermal regelation.
The film is thinner on a particle's cold side, so water keeps flowing from the warm side to the cold side and refreezing, moving the particle toward warmer soil.
A 10-nanometre film around a micrometre-sized particle can move it 10 micrometres a day in a thermal gradient as low as 1 °C m−1.
Regelation purifies growing ice lenses by repelling fine soil particles.

title: Frost-heave landforms
article: Frost heaving#Landforms created by frost heaving

definition.text: Raised-ground features made by frost heaving in circles, polygons and stripes, called palsas in organic soils such as peat and lithalsas in mineral soils.

facts.text: Frost heaves occur in alpine regions even near the equator, as palsas on Mount Kenya show.
Pingos, up to 60 metres high, grow over hundreds of years in Arctic permafrost, fed by upwelling groundwater rather than capillary action.
Small earth hummocks formed by granular convection in seasonally frozen ground are called thúfur in Greenland and Iceland and pounus in Fennoscandia.
In May 2008 the Phoenix lander touched down on polygonal frost-heave ground on Mars and found ice a few centimetres below the surface.

definition.text: The depth to which groundwater in the soil is expected to freeze, also called frost depth or freezing depth.

facts.text: It depends on climate, the heat transfer properties of the soil and nearby materials, and nearby heat sources: snow cover and asphalt insulate, while homes warm the ground.
It deepens toward the poles; maximum frost depth in the contiguous United States ranges from 0 to 8 feet (2.4 m).
In Arctic and Antarctic locations freezing reaches year-round permafrost, and the term thaw depth is used instead.
The frost front is the shifting position of the frost line during seasonal freezing and thawing.
In the tropics, frost line can instead mean the elevation below which frost does not occur.
Building codes put foundations below frost depth because frost heaving can move them; water and sewer pipes are buried below it too.
Where shallow bedrock or utilities prevent deep trenching, pipes may instead be insulated or heated with heat tape.

definition.text: Needle-shaped columns of ice that grow from groundwater at the soil surface, usually on cold nights.

facts.text: It forms when the soil is above 0 °C but the air at the surface is below 0 °C; water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column.
Needles are typically a few centimetres long; 10 cm is the recorded maximum, though 15–20 cm specimens have been seen at Gerðuberg.
It needs ice segregation, in which supercooled water freezes onto existing ice in a porous medium, and it favours soils high in silt and organic matter.
It is frost heaving at the start of the freezing season, before there is any soil overburden to lift.
Growing needles lift soil particles and crusts that settle unevenly on melting, disturbing streambanks, aiding soil creep and shaping patterned ground.
It heaves seedlings out of the ground; they often die because they do not resettle or their roots dry out.
Other names include frost pillars, Kammeis, shimobashira and pipkrake, a Swedish term coined in 1907 by Henrik Hesselman.
Taber found that pore size controls the amount of frost heave and that a gradient of soil moisture tension drives water up toward the freezing front near the surface.

title: Frost boil

definition.text: A small circular mound of fresh soil, also called a mud boil or mud circle, formed by frost action and cryoturbation.

facts.text: Typically 1 to 3 metres across, frost boils occur in periglacial or alpine areas with permafrost and are among the commonest features of patterned ground.
They are nonsorted circles with barren mineral-soil centres and vegetated, peaty ground between them.
Wetter silty or loamy centres grow more ice lenses and heave more than their surroundings, so over years soil is carried upward, a cycle that can take centuries.
In Svalbard, heave at frost boil centres was about 9.5 mm per day against about 1.6 mm per day at their margins.

notes: Formation is explained by several models (cryoturbation, injection, liquefaction); the sources call cryoturbation the most accepted theory without calling the matter disputed.

definition.text: A frost-raised mound in permafrost areas with mineral-rich soils, where a perennial ice lens has grown within the soil.

facts.text: The term sometimes also refers to palsas and pingos.
The stony heaved mounds on the Svalbard archipelago are an example.

title: Patterned ground

definition.text: Distinct, often symmetrical geometric patterns formed by the deformation of ground material in periglacial regions.

facts.text: It occurs wherever soil freezing and thawing alternate, from the Arctic and Antarctica to the Australian Outback, the Atacama Desert and Mars.
Computer models of the past 20 years tie its formation to frost heaving of wet, fine-grained, porous soils.
Repeated freezing and thawing push larger stones up, and lateral forces pile them into clusters and stripes that smooth into polygons, circles and stripes.
Forms include polygons, circles a few centimetres to several metres across, steps, and stripes on slopes of 2° to 7°, each either sorted or unsorted.
Polygons form either in permafrost, as ice wedges, or in areas of seasonal frost.
It forms mostly within the active layer of permafrost.

notes: The Patterned ground article was crawled but sits outside the subject's scope; passes the 2+ pages test (Cryoturbation, Needle ice, Frost boil, Ice wedge, Permafrost, Ice lens).

definition.text: A material's thermal conductivity divided by its density and specific heat capacity, measuring how fast heat spreads through it, in m2/s.

facts.text: The formula is α = k/(ρcp), with k the thermal conductivity, ρ the density and cp the specific heat capacity; ρcp together is the volumetric heat capacity in J/(m3·K).
Heat moves rapidly through a material of high diffusivity because it conducts heat quickly relative to how much energy it stores.
Values in mm2/s include 19 for air at 300 K, 1.15 for sandstone, 1.02 for ice at 0 °C and 0.143 for water at 25 °C.
It is one of the soil thermal properties; the dual-probe heat-pulse sensor measures it in the field together with volumetric heat capacity.

title: Permafrost

definition.text: Soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays continuously below 0 °C for two years or more.

facts.text: The oldest permafrost has been frozen for around 700,000 years; in practice it occurs where the mean annual temperature is 0 °C or below.
It underlies about 11% of the global land surface, around 18 million km2, including much of Alaska, Canada, Greenland and Siberia and high mountains such as the Tibetan Plateau.
Its thickness ranges from below a meter to greater than 1,500 m.
On land it usually lies beneath an active layer of soil that freezes and thaws with the seasons.
Dead biomass has built up in it over millennia without fully decomposing, which makes tundra soil a carbon sink.
As warming thaws it, decomposition restarts and releases carbon dioxide or methane, a climate change feedback.
Thawing ice-rich ground can suddenly exceed hydraulic saturation and shift or collapse, endangering buildings and infrastructure built on it.

conflicts.text: Permafrost base depth reaches 1,493 m in the northern Lena and Yana River basins in Siberia.
conflicts.note: The lead gives the deepest permafrost as greater than 1,500 m; the Classification section says it can exceed 1,400 m (S:cb45bb1e0218).

distinct_from: Revival of ancient organisms from permafrost
notes: Image: the International Permafrost Association map of permafrost extent and types (S:288cf4c9d18e is its caption).

definition.text: The fraction of sunlight a surface reflects, on a scale from 0 (absorbs everything) to 1 (reflects everything).

facts.text: Typical albedos are 0.17 for bare soil, 0.40 for desert sand, 0.15 to 0.18 for deciduous forest and 0.80 for fresh snow.
Low-albedo surfaces look dark and absorb most radiation, while high-albedo surfaces such as snow look bright and reflect most of it.
When snow melts to reveal grass or soil, the darker surface lowers albedo and raises local temperature, causing more melting: a positive feedback.
Farming, deforestation and urbanization change the albedo of large areas.

definition.text: A heating and cooling system for buildings that moves heat to or from the ground, using the near-constant temperature of the earth through the seasons.

facts.text: In the top metre ground temperature follows sunlight and weather; down to about 8–20 m, depending on soil type, swings fade exponentially and lag the surface by about 6 months.
Annual temperature cycles penetrate about 18.0 m in wet clay and 14.5 m in wet sand, but only 6.5 m in dry clay and 4.5 m in dry sand.
Loops in wet ground work better than in dry ground, because water conducts and stores heat better than the solids of sand or soil.
Horizontal loops are laid in trenches deeper than the frost line; efficiency is typically a coefficient of performance of 3–6.

definition.text: The growth of ice lenses where moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone, wedging the material apart.

facts.text: It needs a permeable soil or porous rock, temperatures at which ice and premelted water coexist, and a temperature gradient across the zone.
Where water is plentiful one lens thickens until the heat released by freezing slows it; where water is scarce, new lenses form below, giving multiple layers.
Under high overburden pressure or relatively warm surface temperatures no segregated ice forms and the surface does not deform.
Most frost heaving and bedrock fracture in cold regions comes from ice segregation rather than the expansion of freezing water.

definition.text: Local conditions in the near-surface layer, covering the air just above a surface and the shallow soil and water below, that differ persistently from the surroundings.

facts.text: A microclimate spans a few metres to at most a few kilometres.
Soils that hold moisture damp temperature swings, while soils that dry easily have larger daily changes; clay-rich soils keep heat and moisture near the ground.
Slopes facing the Sun are warmer, while valley bottoms may frost sooner because cold air sinks.
Farmers manage microclimate with irrigation, shading, windbreaks and vegetation to buffer crops from heat and drought.

definition.text: Two laws, posited by Adolf Fick in 1855, that describe diffusion: flux is proportional to the concentration gradient, and concentration changes with time as a result.

facts.text: The first law, J = −D dφ/dx, gives the diffusive flux J from the diffusion coefficient D and the concentration gradient; D has units of area per time.
The second law, ∂φ/∂t = D ∂²φ/∂x², has the same mathematical form as the heat equation.
Fick's law parallels Darcy's law for water flow and Fourier's law for heat, and is used to model transport in porous soils.
Diffusion through porous media may not follow Fick's laws and is then called non-Fickian.

definition.text: The law of heat conduction: the rate of heat flow through a material is proportional to the negative temperature gradient and to the area it crosses.

facts.text: In one dimension the heat flux is q = −k dT/dx, with k the thermal conductivity; the minus sign means heat flows from warmer to cooler regions.
Heat flux is measured in W/m2, with k in W/(m·K) and the gradient in K/m.
Conductivity varies with temperature, with direction in anisotropic materials and with location in non-uniform ones.
Fick's laws of diffusion are its chemical analogue and Ohm's law its electrical one.

definition.text: A partial differential equation, first developed by Joseph Fourier in 1822, that models how temperature in a body changes through time as heat spreads.

facts.text: In three dimensions it reads ∂u/∂t = α(∂²u/∂x² + ∂²u/∂y² + ∂²u/∂z²), with α the thermal diffusivity of the medium.
It says a point heats or cools at a rate proportional to how much hotter or cooler its surroundings are.
The coefficient α combines the material's thermal conductivity, specific heat and density.
For a medium that is not homogeneous and isotropic, α varies with position and the equation takes a slightly different form.

title: Thermal effusivity

definition.text: A material's ability to exchange heat with its surroundings, the square root of its thermal conductivity times its volumetric heat capacity.

facts.text: It measures thermal inertia: a material of low effusivity changes temperature a lot over a day, one of high effusivity much less.
Listed values in kJ/(m2·K·s½) are 0.5–2.6 for soil, 0.63 for dry sand, 1.6 for water and 0.006 for air.
In remote sensing, thermal inertia of a surface reflects particle size, rock abundance, bedrock outcrop and induration.
Diffusivity sets how fast a body reaches thermal equilibrium; effusivity sets how well it resists periodic temperature change.

notes: Table header S:93e6e8a7f353 gives the unit as 'k J m 2 K s' (extraction lost the superscripts); the fact renders it as kJ/(m2·K·s½), the standard unit of effusivity — verification may wish to check.

definition.text: Ground that freezes each winter and thaws again, one of three kinds of frozen ground classed by how long they stay frozen, beside permafrost and pereletok.

facts.text: Repeated freezing and thawing in seasonally frozen areas pushes larger stones toward the surface, forming patterned ground such as polygons.
Cryogenic earth hummocks, formed by granular convection, appear in seasonally frozen ground as well as permafrost.
Rigid retaining-wall footings must sit below the seasonal frost depth.

definition.text: The net movement of atoms, ions, molecules or energy from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration.

facts.text: Diffusion is driven by a gradient in chemical potential, and it differs from bulk flow, which moves a whole body of material down a pressure gradient.
By Fick's first law the diffusive flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient, with the diffusion coefficient D as the constant.
In a porous medium the porosity must be counted in both the flux and accumulation terms; as porosity goes to zero, the molar flux for a given concentration gradient goes to zero.
Under normal conditions molecular diffusion dominates only over lengths from nanometres to millimetres; beyond that convection takes over.

definition.text: A parabolic partial differential equation that describes how the density of a diffusing material changes in space and time.

facts.text: It follows from the continuity equation, which says material is neither created nor destroyed, combined with Fick's first law.
With a constant diffusion coefficient it is linear and identical to the heat equation; if the coefficient depends on density it is nonlinear.
It is the special case of the convection-diffusion equation in which bulk velocity is zero.

definition.text: The amount of heat that must be supplied to an object to raise its temperature by one unit.

facts.text: The SI unit is joule per kelvin; dividing by mass gives specific heat capacity, and dividing by volume gives volumetric heat capacity.
It varies with starting temperature and pressure, and changes sharply at phase transitions such as melting or vaporization.
The heat capacity of a heterogeneous object can usually be found by adding the capacities of its parts.

definition.text: The motion of atoms, molecules or other particles of a gas or liquid at temperatures above absolute zero, which spreads them from high to low concentration.

facts.text: The rate depends on temperature, fluid viscosity and particle size and mass; the result is gradual mixing until the distribution is uniform.
Once concentrations are equal, molecules keep moving in a dynamic equilibrium; chemical diffusion, which needs a gradient, is distinguished from self-diffusion, which does not.
For gases, Fick's law gives the diffusion rate as proportional to the concentration gradient, with a diffusivity that depends on temperature and pressure; it applies where there is no bulk motion.
Molecular diffusion is one of the slower mass-transport mechanisms.

definition.text: The pressure a single gas in a mixture would exert if it alone filled the whole volume at the same temperature.

facts.text: By Dalton's law, the total pressure of an ideal gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its gases.
The partial pressure of a component equals its mole fraction times the total pressure, and its mole fraction equals its volume fraction.
Gases dissolve, diffuse and react according to their partial pressures, not their concentrations in a mixture or solution.
For non-ideal gases the concept generalises to fugacity.

definition.text: A measure of a material's intrinsic ability to conduct heat locally, in watts per metre-kelvin.

facts.text: Conduction is energy transport by random molecular motion across a temperature gradient, without macroscopic flows; heat flows from high to low temperature.
Methods are steady-state, which wait for a steady temperature profile, or transient, which use the system as it approaches steady state.
A phase change can alter conductivity abruptly: ice at 0 °C conducts at 2.18 W/(m·K), liquid water at 0.56.
Without convection, air and other gases are good insulators, so insulating materials work by trapping many gas-filled pockets that block conduction.
Conductivity can differ with direction in some materials, for example wood conducts better along the grain than across it.

definition.text: A gas in an atmosphere that absorbs the heat a planet radiates and so raises its surface temperature.

facts.text: Without greenhouse gases Earth's average surface temperature would be about -18 °C instead of the present 15 °C.

Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of dry air, barely absorb infrared; carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and other trace gases, under 0.1% of the atmosphere, absorb it because their molecules are asymmetric in charge.

Water vapour causes 41-67% of the greenhouse effect, but its short residence time of about nine days means human activity barely changes it globally; it amplifies warming through water vapour feedback.
Concentrations follow the balance of sources and sinks; the soil, oceans and vegetation are sinks, and about 0.55 of emitted CO2 is absorbed by land and ocean sinks in the first year.

Most human CO2 comes from fossil fuels, with additions from cement, fertiliser production and land-use change; agriculture is a major methane source, and rice paddies give 22% of agricultural methane and 11% of nitrous oxide.

title: Global warming potential
article: Greenhouse gas#Global warming potential (GWP) and CO2 equivalents

definition.text: A dimensionless measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a chosen period, as a multiple of the warming from the same mass of CO2.

facts.text: CO2 has a GWP of 1 by definition; for other gases it depends on how strongly the gas absorbs thermal radiation, how fast it leaves the atmosphere and the time frame.
Methane has a 20-year GWP of 81.2, so a tonne of methane leaked equals 81.2 tonnes of CO2 over that period.

definition.text: A geographic area whose climate, soil and farming practices favour producing particular crops, plants or livestock.

facts.text: A region may be dominated by one crop, such as the American Corn Belt, or be diverse where soil fertility and seasonal rainfall are high, as in Queensland and New South Wales.
Cultivation may be enabled by a regional climate or a unique microclimate, and regions are often aligned along a latitude because crops need consistent climate.
